content: 1. The bioavailability of the 50 mg delamanid tablet may be altered if the tablet is split, crushed, or dissolved. Delamanid is sensitive to oxidation and heat, so retaining pill fragments for later use may result in reduced delivery of the active compound and the formation of unspecified oxidation by-products. 2. Avoiding injectable-containing regimens is particularly desirable in children, especially those who are very young, have mild disease (as indicated by the absence of malnutrition), or lack serious forms of extrapulmonary disease, cavitation on chest radiography, or HIV infection. 3. Hearing loss in children can have a permanent impact on language acquisition and learning ability. Therefore, if amikacin or streptomycin is used in children, regular audiometry is required to monitor for potential hearing damage. 4. Recommendations on treatment duration also apply to children, subject to their response to treatment. Shortening the total treatment duration to less than 18 months may be considered for children without extensive disease. 5. WHO recommendations for longer MDR-TB regimens also apply to patients with extrapulmonary TB and TB meningitis. Adjustments may be required depending on the specific location of the disease. 6. Treatment of MDR/RR-TB meningitis should be guided by drug susceptibility testing (DST) of the infecting strain and knowledge of the properties of TB medicines that cross the blood-brain barrier. Levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, ethionamide, prothionamide, cycloserine, terizidone, linezolid, and imipenem-cilastatin penetrate the CNS well. However, seizures may be more common in children treated with imipenem-cilastatin, so meropenem is preferred in such cases. 7. High-dose isoniazid and pyrazinamide can reach therapeutic levels in cerebrospinal fluid and may be useful if the strains are susceptible. In contrast, p-aminosalicylic acid and ethambutol do not penetrate the CNS well and should not be relied upon for MDR/RR-TB meningitis. Amikacin and streptomycin penetrate the CNS only in the presence of meningeal inflammation. 8. There is limited data on the CNS penetration of clofazimine, bedaquiline, or delamanid. Additionally, cerebrospinal fluid concentrations may not accurately reflect concentrations in the meninges or brain. 9. Amikacin, streptomycin, prothionamide, and ethionamide are generally contraindicated during pregnancy. Knowledge about the safety of bedaquiline and delamanid in pregnancy and breastfeeding is sparse, though observational data from South Africa on 58 mothers who received bedaquiline during pregnancy showed no significant differences in infant or maternal outcomes. 10. In cases where bedaquiline and delamanid are used during pregnancy, longer regimens should be individualized to include components with better-established safety profiles. Outcomes of treatment and pregnancy, including postpartum surveillance for congenital anomalies, should be documented to inform future recommendations. 11. The concurrent use of bedaquiline and delamanid has insufficient evidence regarding efficacy or effectiveness. However, safety data suggest no additional safety concerns, and their use may be considered in patients with limited treatment options due to extensive drug resistance or intolerance to other second-line TB medications. 12. Safety monitoring, including baseline and ongoing ECG and electrolyte monitoring, is essential for patients receiving bedaquiline and delamanid. Clinicians should be aware of other QT-prolonging medications in the regimen and the long half-life of bedaquiline, which persists in tissues beyond its use. 13. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) is critical to ensure the effectiveness of MDR/RR-TB regimens. Rapid diagnostic testing can help clinicians determine eligibility for specific regimens and select appropriate agents. Empirical treatment may need to be initiated before DST results are available, with adjustments made once results are obtained. 14. When DST indicates resistance to a specific agent, it is better to replace that agent. This also applies to medicines for which DST methods are unreliable for clinical decision-making. 15. The design of MDR/RR-TB regimens must balance the benefits and harms to the individual patient, including potential drug-drug interactions, toxicity, and pill burden. 16. Updated weight-based dosage schedules for MDR-TB medicines were introduced in 2018 for both children and adults, based on the latest knowledge and expert consultation. Adherence to these schedules is advised whenever possible. 17. Monitoring and evaluation of patients on longer MDR-TB regimens are essential. This includes clinical and laboratory testing, such as audiometry, visual acuity tests, and ECG, to assess treatment response and safety. 18. Persistent culture positivity beyond the expected timeframe should prompt a review of the regimen and DST performance. National TB programs should aim for complete registration and follow-up of MDR/RR-TB patients as part of national surveillance. 19. Systematic monitoring of adverse events during and after treatment needs strengthening in most national TB programs, given the increasing use of new and repurposed medications in MDR/RR-TB regimens. 20. Prospective collection of accurate case-based data using electronic registers is strongly advised to benefit individual patients and inform revisions of local and global policies.
